doc.title: Keter Betts interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 11, 1996

title: Segregated dance halls in the South
summary: At dances with Bostic and Dinah, halls roped off sections by race, and young people cut the ropes to join the music.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: I had one last question. When you were playing dances like with Dinah Washington or with Bostic, were these segregated clubs or how did they work?
The dance halls in the south?
Oh yeah, they were segregated. They put a rope up.
They put a rope down the middle.

Not down the middle, down the side. They made the nucleus of it for the blacks to dance, and they’d have a rope on the side, and they’d cut the rope. And the kids back then, they’d put up another rope, and after they’d cut the rope and they’d be out. I mean this was all the time. Because that’s when I really got a chance to look at that whole situation and I’m not looking at the political side, I’m looking at the musical side, that these people enjoyed this music and wanted to be a part of it. But they were the ones that were being denied. I mean to a certain point it was the reverse. They were being denied the privilege of just being able to stand and look. But how can you stand in middle, and everybody’s out there having fun, and don’t move—
